extracted.intended_audience: science policymakers, research administrators, and scientists concerned with research-funding and peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the defects of competitive grant peer review systems (NSF/NIH-style) and principles for designing alternative research-funding mechanisms. Includes a concrete proposal (modified block grants) that operationalizes those principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive opportunity cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Top scientists spend 25–50% of their time writing and reviewing grants rather than doing research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates a funding system by how much productive research time it diverts into proposal-writing and peer review; lower opportunity cost is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservatism / aversion to high-risk high-payoff work
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers favor proposals where the answer is essentially known, creating bias against high-risk, high-payoff research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A desirable funding system should tolerate failure and not systematically penalize risky proposals that could yield major advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias against young investigators
rubrics_metrics.description: Young researchers lacking established track records are disadvantaged by competitive peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether allocation mechanisms disadvantage early-career scientists and whether corrective measures exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias against established scientists changing fields
rubrics_metrics.description: An established scientist's track record in one field does not carry over when they change fields, producing unfair disadvantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the system recognizes transferable expertise and supports productive field changes rather than penalizing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias against interdisciplinary work
rubrics_metrics.description: Interdisciplinary proposals that don't fit cleanly into a single review panel are disadvantaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how well funding processes handle cross-disciplinary work and whether organizational structures force ill-fitting categorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Mission" work crowds out curiosity-driven inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Programmatic or mission-oriented funding priorities can reduce support for basic curiosity-driven science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the balance of mission-directed versus investigator-initiated funding and the system's capacity to preserve exploratory research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicts of interest among reviewers are pervasive but under-managed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the extent to which conflicts are declared, managed, or mitigated; systems that reduce concentrated power can reduce conflict impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer competence is variable and not audited
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers' expertise varies and the system lacks mechanisms to audit or ensure reviewer competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good systems should include processes to assess reviewer qualifications, track review quality, or otherwise provide accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity prevents applicants from countering errors of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymity in review prevents applicants from responding to factual errors in reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider transparency and rebuttal opportunities; mechanisms enabling applicant response improve fairness and factual accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: System rewards proposal-writing skill rather than scientific ability
rubrics_metrics.description: Success depends heavily on rhetorical/proposal-writing skill rather than demonstrated scientific accomplishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer allocation methods that weight demonstrated past output over polished proposal-writing; reduce incentives to prioritize grantmanship over research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize time scientists spend on funding paperwork
rubrics_metrics.description: A better funding system should minimize the amount of time scientists devote to proposal-writing and administrative paperwork.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize by reducing application/reporting burdens, simplifying processes, or providing baseline funding that obviates frequent proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerate failure — fund risky work
rubrics_metrics.description: A desirable system tolerates failure and funds high-risk, high-payoff research rather than only safe, incremental projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design incentives and allocation rules that allow for a portfolio including higher-risk projects and accept a higher failure rate as part of progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocate based on demonstrated past output, not rhetorical proposal quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions should be based on demonstrable past scientific output rather than persuasive proposal rhetoric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metrics or peer-recognition mechanisms that weight past accomplishments and evidence of productivity over proposal polish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribute decision-making power widely rather than concentrating it in panels
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision authority should be widely distributed across the scientific community instead of concentrated in anonymous review panels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wider distribution can reduce bottlenecks, conflicts of interest, and conservatism; consider decentralizing allocation authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build in self-correction through peer recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: A funding system should enable self-correction by allowing peers to recognize and support valuable work (peer-recognition-by-action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms that let scientists allocate resources to colleagues (e.g., redistribution requirements) create ongoing local feedback and reputational correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modified Block Grants (Roy's alternative mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every qualified scientist receives a guaranteed baseline of funding; additional discretionary funds are distributed by individual scientists themselves to colleagues whose work they value, with each scientist required to redistribute a fraction of what they receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mechanism shifts allocation from anonymous panels to peer-recognition-by-action, aims to minimize paperwork, tolerate risk, allocate on demonstrated output, distribute decision-making widely, and create self-correction. Assess implementation details such as baseline size, required redistribution fraction, eligibility, and safeguards against collusion or concentrated capture.
